transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-29
Start: 14:30 PST
Duration: 52 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Jordan Morales, Priya Shah (Redwood) — Ethan Park, Maya Singh, Carlos Ruiz (SolarWind)
Recording ID: ff-20251229-solarwind-sdk-01

Summary: Quickstart walkthrough of Redwood SDKs (Python + TypeScript), auth patterns for sandbox and CI, environment setup for VPC/private deployment considerations, and Optimize recommendations for batching/quantization. Agreed to run a benchmark matrix in Jan and exchange security artifacts.

Topics:
- SDK quickstart steps (py/ts)
- Auth: API keys vs OIDC/GCP Workload Identity vs SAML SSO
- Environment: sandbox, CI secret rotation, VPC peering, KMS integration
- Console walkthrough: routes, token breakouts, per-route dashboards
- Redwood Optimize: batching, quantization suggestions by workload

Action items (quick inline): Jordan to send pricing; Priya to share repos and sandbox; Maya to send VPC diagram.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: All right hello everybody, this is Jordan from Redwood Inference. Thanks for joining, we have Priya with me. Um, quick roll call?
[00:08] Ethan: Hey this is Ethan, lead ML eng at SolarWind.
[00:11] Maya: Maya here, platform.
[00:13] Carlos: Carlos, CTO.
[00:15] Priya: Priya, Solutions Eng - I'll run the SDK bits and the Optimize demo.
[00:18] Jordan: Great. High level agenda: quick SDK quickstart (py + ts), auth patterns and CI, then console and Optimize, then Q&A. We'll share the slide deck and quickstart repos after.
[00:30] Ethan: Sounds good, our main goals — low latency for customer-facing features, and keep inference cost reasonable. Also we have regulatory constraints in EU and some PII issues so VPC or private deployment is possible.
[00:42] Jordan: Yep totally, that maps to hosted vs dedicated vs private in Redwood. We'll discuss tradeoffs.
[00:48] Maya: Our infra is mainly GCP, k8s, using GKE autopilot, and we use Cloud KMS. CI runs in GitLab.
[00:56] Priya: Perfect, we have documented patterns for GCP workload identity + KMS. For CI we recommend ephemeral keys and the SDK supports env var tokens + a short-lived token flow. We'll show sample CI snippet in a sec.

[01:12] [Priya screen share: quickstart repo]
[01:15] Priya: Ok starting with Python quickstart — pip install redwood-inference (note: package name may be auto-corrected in transcript), set REDWOOD_API_KEY in env, example: from redwood import Client; client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')); resp = client.generate("... ")
[01:33] Ethan: Is there a managed SDK for streaming responses? We need partial tokens for typing indicators.
[01:38] Priya: Yes, streaming is supported via the SDK — in Python use client.stream_generate(...) and in TS we have an async iterator. We also have websocket and chunked HTTP fallback.
[01:48] Jordan: For the TypeScript quickstart, Priya will paste the snippet — it's on the repo: npm i @redwood/inference; import { Redwood } from '@redwood/inference'...
[01:56] Priya: Quick auth note — you can use long-lived API keys for low-friction dev, but for production we prefer OIDC / short-lived tokens. If you're on GCP, Workload Identity is simplest; otherwise we support OIDC and SAML via your idp.
[02:10] Maya: For CI rotation, is there a recommended cadence? We rotate secrets every 30 days, so we need automation.
[02:16] Priya: We have a sample GitLab CI job that exchanges a service account token for a short-lived Redwood token; you can use our token-exchange endpoint. We'll share the snippet in the quickstart repo, and include a sample terraform module.
[02:30] Carlos: On the private deployment side, are audit logs forwarded to our SIEM? That's a hard ask from compliance.
[02:36] Jordan: Yes, Private has KMS and audit log forwarding. For hosted we provide audit logs and retention add-ons; for Dedicated/Private we can forward to your Splunk/BigQuery - we'll include the doc.

[02:50] [00:02:50] Priya: Moving to environment setup. I'll walk through the sandbox flow: 1) we provision a sandbox org and issue a scoped API key tied to a project, 2) you can upload sample data (or point to a GCS bucket with read-only perms), 3) configure routes in Console, 4) run quick benchmark or perf test.
[03:10] Ethan: About data: we need to ensure customer PII doesn't leave our control. Can you do GPU inference where input never persists?
[03:18] Priya: Yes — we have TTL for request logs and an option to disable logging for particular routes, plus redaction. On Dedicated/Private you own the data plane. Hosted has SOC 2 controls and you can opt into retention settings.

[03:35] [03:35] Jordan: Let's demo the Console: per-route token cost breakdown, latency percentiles, and the Optimize suggestions tab which will recommend batching and quantization settings. Priya, you want to drive?
[03:44] Priya: Sure. (click) Here is the Routes view — you can pin a model variant and set rollout policies. On the right we show token cost and top input sizes. Optimize suggests an appropriate batch size given your 95th percentile latency requirement; for high-throughput batch endpoints we recommend a max batch of 32 with KV cache enabled.
[04:05] Maya: The Optimize suggestions — are those rules or just heuristics? We want reproducible configs.
[04:09] Priya: A mix: heuristics from workload profiling + a rule engine that simulates SLOs against cost. You can accept suggestions or run an A/B rollout. The suggestions are deterministic per profile and we annotate the expected cost delta.

[04:25] [04:25] Ethan: Can we run an in-house benchmark? Our team measures tail latency under 99th percentile; we need both worst-case and median.
[04:31] Priya: Absolutely. Typical next step is a benchmark matrix: examples of prompts, typical seq len, concurrency pattern. We'll run both hosted and dedicated profiles. If you want private, we can provide an on-prem package — though that's heavier.
[04:45] Carlos: Cost — can you give a rough per-1M-token comparison for hosted vs dedicated?
[04:50] Jordan: We'll send a matrix; short answer: hosted is easier for eval but can be ~20-40% higher for steady-state; Dedicated gives lower unit cost with commitments. Exact numbers depend on quantization and batching.

[05:05] [05:05] Priya: Jumping into the TypeScript quickstart now — note the sample uses node-fetch for streaming; example code for typed responses and function/tool calling is in the repo. Also mention: we have SDK validators for response shape to reduce runtime errors.
[05:21] Ethan: Do you support function calling / tooling patterns like OpenAI's format?
[05:25] Priya: We do similar structured output and function calling; interoperability is usually straightforward but there are minor differences in schema names. We'll include a migration guide in the repo.
[05:36] Maya: About VPC peering — our security team wants private egress, no public internet. Is there an option?
[05:42] Jordan: For Private or Dedicated in VPC mode, traffic stays in your VPC. For hosted, we can do private peering in some regions — we'll need your network diagram to confirm.
[05:52] Maya: Ok I'll send that.

[06:00] [06:00] Priya: Now a quick live dev demo: I run the Python sample generating a summary for a 800-token input. (typing) The response comes back; streaming chunks arrive approx every 120ms in this small test. Note — in heavy load you'll see batching which increases per-request latency but reduces token cost.
[06:25] Ethan: Do you have adaptive batching that prefers latency SLOs over cost?
[06:29] Priya: Yes, you can set SLO-first policy and our runtime reduces batching to meet the latency SLO; cost goes up accordingly. There's also a cost-first policy that accepts higher latency to save tokens.

[06:45] [06:45] Jordan: Let's surface some of the typical pitfalls — 1) using a single long-lived key in CI, 2) not sizing batch maxs which causes tail latency spikes, 3) forgetting to pin model versions during rollout.
[06:58] Priya: Also watch out for tokenization mismatch if you switch models; we surface a tokenizer compare tool in the Console.

[07:10] [07:10] Ethan: One of our customers needs EU residency — can Redwood guarantee EU-only inference for hosted?
[07:15] Jordan: We have regional hosting and can route requests to EU regions and ensure logs are stored in region depending on retention settings. For strict residency you can go Private in an EU DC. We'll include our data residency doc.

[07:30] [07:30] Carlos: Security questions: SOC 2 and ISO? KMS? HSM?
[07:35] Jordan: We are SOC 2 Type II and pursuing ISO; KMS integration supported (Cloud KMS, AWS KMS). For HSM-backed keys in Private setups that's possible — we'll send the security pack.

[07:52] [07:52] Priya: Quick demo of Optimize output — I'm opening a sample route profile. It recommends 8-bit quantization for this model at ~2% quality delta but 3x lower memory. For conversation workloads with short seq lengths it recommends aggressive batching with cache.
[08:12] Maya: How do you measure the quality delta? Do you run our eval sets?
[08:16] Priya: We run a small set of prompts from your eval set; we'll ask you to provide a representative prompt set for more accurate measurements. Quality regressions are tied to alerts in the Console.

[08:33] [08:33] Jordan: Ok let's go through an example CI snippet I mentioned earlier — Priya can paste.
[08:38] Priya: (reads) script: - curl -X POST https://auth.redwood.ai/exchange -d @service-account.jwt | jq -r .short_token; export REDWOOD_API_KEY=... then run test. In GitLab we put the token in a masked variable and use a short lived token. We also include a sample for GitHub Actions.
[08:58] Ethan: Good. Our SREs want to audit all token exchanges. Is there an audit log for token issuance?
[09:03] Priya: Yes, token issuance is logged and can be forwarded to your audit store for Private/Dedicated; hosted customers can subscribe to audit log exports.

[09:15] [09:15] Jordan: Quick question from the chat — do we support custom plugins or lightweight retriever integration?
[09:20] Priya: We support retrieval-augmented generation via a connector framework; you can plug in vector DBs and we support embedding pipelines. We'll share our RAG connector examples in the repo.

[09:35] [09:35] Maya: Any regional limitations for GPUs and model variants? We need certain model families only available on certain instance types.
[09:41] Priya: Yes, instance availability varies by region; we publish a model-hosting matrix in the Console. For Dedicated you can request specific GPU families in your reserved fleet.

[09:55] [09:55] Ethan: Let's talk about fallback strategies — if the model variant is out of capacity, what happens?
[10:00] Priya: Smart routing will fallback to a compatible variant based on cost/latency policy. You can configure automatic fallback to a smaller model with graceful degradation.

[10:14] [10:14] Jordan: We're approaching the middle of the call; any outstanding red flags?
[10:18] Carlos: The main ones: data residency confirmation, audit log forwarding, and a quantifiable cost estimate for our 1M monthly tokens baseline.
[10:26] Jordan: Noted. We'll get the pricing matrix plus a worked example in tokens per feature.

[10:35] [10:35] Priya: I'll walk through a short Optimize run: upload a sample workload, pick latency target, it simulates cost and generates config changes — batch size, kv cache enable, quantization. (shares screen) For a 50ms median SLO and 1s 99p SLO, Optimize suggests batch 8 and 8-bit quantization for this 6B model.
[10:55] Maya: Can Optimize automatically roll out the change to production?
[10:59] Priya: We support canary rollouts and A/B splits. Auto-rollout we'd recommend gating behind alerts.

[11:10] [11:10] Ethan: For our benchmark, what artifacts do you need from us?
[11:14] Priya: Representative prompt set, average and 95th seq lengths, concurrency pattern, desired latency SLOs, and target cost metric. We'll also ask for a small eval set for quality checks.

[11:28] [11:28] Jordan: Let's capture next steps — I'll send pricing and the security pack, Priya will share repos and sandbox invite. Can we agree the benchmark week of Jan 12?
[11:36] Ethan: Yes, that works.
[11:38] Carlos: We'll aim to provide the prompt sets and VPC diagram by Jan 5.

[11:46] [11:46] Priya: I'll create a sandbox org and invite Ethan + Maya. Expect an email from me with repo links and the quickstart checklist.

[12:00] [12:00] Jordan: Any final questions?
[12:03] Maya: One quick one — recovery/fallback: do you provide rate-limiting and burst protection?
[12:08] Priya: Yes rate-limiting per token and burst policies are configurable per route. We also expose per-token cost metrics to connect to your upstream throttles.

[12:18] [12:18] Ethan: Great, thanks for the walk-through.
[12:21] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with links.

References / shared artifacts mentioned: Quickstart repos (https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-quickstart - note: sample link), Sandbox invite (sent by Priya), Security pack (link_to_security_docs.pdf), Benchmark spreadsheet (https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/benchmark-example).

End transcript.
